content: 1. Kranzler K conducted a systematic review to identify risk factors, barriers, and facilitators for linking individuals to antiretroviral therapy (ART) care. The findings were published in the journal AIDS in 2012, volume 26, pages 2059–2067. 2. Zulliger R, Black S, Holtgrave DR, Ciaranello AL, Bekker LG, and Myer L evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a package of interventions aimed at expediting ART initiation during pregnancy in Cape Town, South Africa. Their study was published in AIDS Behavior in 2014, volume 18, pages 697–705. 3. Long L, Maskew M, Brennan A, Mongwenyana C, Nyoni C, Malete G, and colleagues assessed the cost-effectiveness of same-day treatment initiation in South Africa. Their findings were presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) in Seattle, WA, USA, from February 13–16, 2017. 4. The International Treatment Preparedness Coalition posed the question of whether ART should be offered on the same day as diagnosis. This topic was discussed on their website, accessed on May 19, 2017. 5. Protopopescu C, Carrieri M, Raffi F, Hardel L, Sobel A, Perronne C, and colleagues demonstrated the persistent effect of early adherence (at month 4) to ART on long-term virological response in HIV-infected patients. This was based on a 12-year follow-up of the ANRS C08 APROCO-COPILOTE cohort. The results were presented at the 8th IAS Conference on HIV Pathogenesis, Treatment, and Prevention in Vancouver, Canada, from July 19–22, 2015 (Abstract TUPEB291). 6. Archary M, Sartorius B, La Russa P, Sibaya T, Healey M, Bobat R, and colleagues compared early versus delayed ART initiation in HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition. Their findings were presented at the CROI in Seattle, WA, USA, from February 13–16, 2017 (Abstract 817LB). 7. Kim MH, Cox C, Dave A, Draper HR, Kabue M, Schutze GE, and colleagues found that prompt initiation of ART combined with therapeutic food improved outcomes in HIV-infected Malawian children with malnutrition. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2012, volume 59, pages 173–176. 8. Njuguna N, Cranmer L, Otieno V, Okinya H, Benki-Nugent S, Stern J, and colleagues conducted a randomized trial comparing urgent versus post-stabilization ART initiation in hospitalized children. The results were presented at the CROI in Boston, MA, USA, from February 22–25, 2016. 9. The use of Xpert® MTB/RIF is strongly recommended as the initial diagnostic test for HIV-associated tuberculosis (TB) or multidrug-resistant TB, rather than conventional microscopy, culture, and drug susceptibility testing. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence for adults, adolescents, and children. 10. Xpert® MTB/RIF is also recommended for diagnosing TB meningitis using cerebrospinal fluid specimens, with strong recommendations based on very low-quality evidence for all age groups. 11. The LF-LAM test may assist in diagnosing active TB in adults living with HIV who have a CD4 count ≤100 cells/mm³ or are seriously ill, regardless of CD4 count. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 12. Routine serum or plasma cryptococcal antigen screening is conditionally recommended for ART-naïve adults with a CD4 count <100 cells/mm³ before ART initiation. This is based on low-quality evidence. 13. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is strongly recommended for individuals with severe or advanced HIV clinical disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) or a CD4 count <350 cells/mm³. This recommendation is supported by moderate-quality evidence. 14. Isoniazid preventive therapy is strongly recommended for individuals unlikely to have active TB, based on symptom screening, regardless of tuberculin skin test status, ART status, or pregnancy. This recommendation is supported by high-quality evidence. 15. Pre-emptive antifungal therapy with fluconazole is conditionally recommended for individuals with positive cryptococcal antigen screening and a CD4 count <100 cells/mm³, provided lumbar puncture excludes cryptococcal meningitis. This recommendation is based on low-quality evidence. 16. The WHO guideline development process included a thorough review of conflicts of interest, with all contributors completing declarations of interest forms. The results were reviewed and managed according to WHO policy, ensuring transparency and minimizing bias. 17. Evidence synthesis for the guidelines relied on key information sources, including systematic reviews, expert consultations, and data from clinical trials. The GRADE methodology was used to assess the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations.
